doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Guitar history and the classical divide
title: Guitarmania in the early nineteenth century and the classical canon
summary: Juber argues that early nineteenth-century guitarists were popular musicians sidelined by the classical canon, naming Legnani, Sor, Aguado, Mertz and others.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: I don’t consider analysis to be the province of classical. We associate music education with classical because we use the classical canon as the core of that repertoire. But because of being a guitar player, and the guitar is not considered truly part of the classical canon, other than the Segovia paradigm, the Spanish classical guitar which Segovia succeeded in bringing the gravitas and putting it in the concert hall. But what he represented in terms of the guitar was a pretty narrow focus. Even within his own paradigm it’s a pretty narrow focus. But you go back to the early nineteenth century when there was guitarmania in Europe, in fact my presentation I call “Guitarmania to Beatlemania” because the guitar was extremely important in music-making. I mean Berlioz, Schubert, Diabelli, Musicalis, to name a few, Hummel, they’re all guitar players. Schubert wrote many of his songs on guitar. The music that was published, there’s an enormous amount of pieces that were published. The levels of virtuosity — Legnani, Italian guitar player, was the Paginini of the guitar, and did concerts with Paginini. In fact the story is that they had a concert piece that they had performed together, and toward the end they’d swap instruments. Because Paginini was a guitar player too. I think the only pieces that he wrote that didn’t include a guitar were the 24 Caprice. And then Legnani wrote 36 Caprice, in every key, that are fiendishly difficult. But the virtuosi, not just

guitar virtuosi but virtuosi in general outside of that strict classical canon, they were not included. And the level of musicianship that — it is very tangible. That it wasn’t just that they were developing technique. Aguado, who is pretty much the father of modern classical guitar technique, he was kind of the pedagogue, really the principal pedagogue. Fernando Sor, for example, was a very accomplished composer. He was a songwriter, he wrote a vocal method, he wrote a guitar method. He played guitar with really a technique more akin to lute technique than modern guitar technique. But his method starts with harmony. Now he is not considered classical in the sense of being part of the canon. But in that late Classical/early Romantic era, they were extremely accomplished. And where is the division between the C major chord that is classical or jazz or pop or rock? There is none. The meta information does not change. And who can improvise? Not the classical musicians, mostly, because they never learned. There are guitar players that go four years of conservatory training and can’t string a chord sequence together. But those musicians were expected to. They were all expected to improvise, they have to read figured bass, all of that stuff. So I think that in a sense, the designation of classical theory really it just puts things too much in a box. So my experience is that music is music and it doesn’t matter what the stylistic context is. Obviously one needs to study the classics. But I was having a conversation yesterday with somebody who had done some kind of event about who was the better composer, Handel or Bach. And I started thinking about that and realized that you know Handel was a commercial composer. Bach was a utility composer. He composed for his patrons and he composed for the church. But Handel wrote commercial music. And the opera composers of the nineteenth century were the commercial songwriters of that era, much in the same way as for example, I will take a Beatles song and arrange it. Well the early Romantic guitar players, the guitarmania era people and really between the French revolution and the 1848 revolution, that period really, the first half of the nineteenth century, they were accomplished in all those parameters that we associate with classical music. But it’s only a footnote in the history books. So what my position is, fine. You don’t want to call it classical? It’s popular music. They arranged opera tunes. They wrote their own compositions. Johann Caspar Mertz for example, was the Schumann of the guitar. I mean his music is incredibly impressionistic in the stuff that he was writing in the 1830s and 1840. But always very guitaristic. Zani deFerranti was an Italian guitarist. Berlioz said, “he rocks you,” literally that’s what Berlioz said. So he was the first rock guitar player. And so they’re not considered, I mean in the classical guitar world yes, it’s a label. You can say these are classical guitar players. But in their era they weren’t. And to my mind they do what I do. They toured, they were the first international touring musicians. A lot of guitar players toured internationally. They arranged pop songs. They wrote their own music. They did
method books, they published, they made their money, as much as they could, on publishing. Diabelli published an enormous amount of guitar music.
